subtopic: MR. GRAFFTEY-STATEMENT BEFORE STANDING COMMITTEE RESPECTING BRIBES
MR. GRAFFTEY-STATEMENT BEFORE STANDING COMMITTEE RESPECTING BRIBES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak briefly on a question of privilege affecting all members of this house. I realize the seriousness of questions of privilege; this is only the second occasion on which I have raised one since I first entered this chamber nearly nine years ago.
Yesterday, one Philip J. Farmer, an executive director of the Canadian Highway Safety Council, appeared before the committee on justice and legal affairs, and according to verified reports he said that in the past I had suggested that the Canadian Highway Safety Council had accepted bribes and silencing money from the automobile industry. Mr. Speaker, at no time in the past, and in no place, did I use the words "bribes" or "silencing money".
I said I would be brief, sir, and I will be brief. I have said during the last two years that for some time the Canadian Highway Safety Council had done a reasonably good job in cajoling the driver, and talking about roads, but only recently in the last 18 months has it been prodded into discussing the car in the safety debate on highway deaths and accidents. The reason for its failure, I said, was because it had excluded the car from the debate.
Mr. Farmer said yesterday that in 1966 the Canadian Highway Safety Council received only 9.4 per cent of its total contributions from the automobile industry. He did not mention the amounts received from allied industries-finance companies, tire companies and parts companies. I have only pointed out that there was a conflict of interest upon the Canadian Highway Safety Council inasmuch as those who make up the council and are responsible for its direction are, in their day to day work, attached to the automobile industry or to allied industries.
[DOT] (11:10 a.m.)
The president of the Canadian Highway Safety Council is president of Industrial Acceptance Corporation which finances automobile purchases. Another director is president of White Motor Company. Mr. Arch Bryce, who for years was executive secretary of the Canadian Highway Safety Council, is now a safety adviser to the Ford Motor Company, and, Mr. Speaker, he did not get this job by bringing the automobile into the safety debate.
I conclude by saying that instead of splitting hairs before the legal and justice committee the safety council should be advertising conditions regarding the defective automobiles on the road in Canada today. As the chief commoner in the land and as protector of our rights and privileges I suggest to Your Honour that this witness be called again, either before the legal and justice committee or before the house committee on privileges, and be made to testify as to the time and place that I ever used the words "bribes" or "silencing money". If he cannot produce this testimony, which I know he cannot, he should be severely censured by the proper authorities in the house for putting words into my mouth that I did not use.

subtopic: MR. GRAFFTEY-STATEMENT BEFORE STANDING COMMITTEE RESPECTING BRIBES
speechtext: Hear, hear.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to repeat my question to the Minister of Transport which I put to him last Friday and which is recorded on page 10047 of Hansard in regard to the removal of English speaking telephone operators in the government employ. The Minister of Transport replied that he knew of no such action but would look into the matter. I have not received a reply since then.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to associate myself with the hon. member for Prince Ed-ward-Lennox who last night pointed out in the house so ably that the Canadian people are wondering just what is going on in the country today and what is the objective of the Liberal government. Today in Canada 67 per cent of the population is English speaking, whether of English or other ethnic or g.n, and one by one they are being removed from the service of the government. The people of Canada are fed up with this state of affairs. It is time we were informed of the objective of this government, and of their action in this respect.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to reply to the hon. gentleman at once by saying that these employees are not civil servants but employees of the Bell Telephone Company. We have told that company that every employee of the government switchboard must be English speaking. If they cannot answer the telephone in English, they cannot be employed.

November 25, 1966
Supply-Transport
We think that since there are two official languages in this country it is right that any one who places a call through the government switchboard in the other official language should receive a reply in that language as well. I think this is only fair. All this means is that we want operators who can answer the telephone on the government switchboard in either of the two official languages. They may be born in Poland, they may be born in Saskatchewan or they may be born in China, but it is a requirement that they be able to answer simple questions in both official languages. If we are going to have a united country it seems to me we can ask for no less.
[DOT] (11:40 a.m.)

I want to be as fair about this as I can, Mr. Chairman, but we are living in the province of Ontario, and a check of 9,000 telephone calls, made by us, revealed that 7,221 were answered in French. We are still living in Ontario, in this part of Canada. What is the reason for this?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
If the hon. member will bring to my notice a single instance that he knows of himself, or that anyone else knows of, where somebody has telephoned the government switchboard and has found that the operator cannot answer in English I shall take the matter up at once with as much indignation as he shows. It is absolutely imperative that every operator on the government switchboard be able to answer in English. It is equally important that those who wish to speak in the other official language be answered in the other official language, without having to have a second operator searched for. Because of this, employees not qualified are simply being transferred from the government switchboard by the Bell Telephone Company to other employment at the same remuneration, and no injustice is involved in this.
I think it is elementary justice, if you are to have two official languages in this country, that a person can telephone the government switchboard, make his request in either official language, and receive a prompt reply.

I do not want anyone to think that the sentiment I express comes from this side of the house only. The minister is well aware of what happened in his own caucus this week, and I want him to keep that in mind.
On a question of privilege-

Nevertheless I am glad to have this opportunity to make these few comments on the estimates of the Department of Transport. I am disappointed, first of all, that the minister has not seen fit to make a statement. I would be very interested to know what his feelings are with respect to a number of questions. I wish to say a few words, myself, about those matters, and about one, in particular, which has received very little attention recently. I have in mind the announcement made by the minister on March 25, 1965, that assistance to local airports would be forthcoming.
I was happy to hear the minister make this announcement. I have felt for many years that since we support automobilists by providing them with roads out of public taxation it would be no more than justice to provide airports for people in outlying areas, in particular, who want to fly planes and land them safely, instead of being obliged to use rough fields and makeshift facilities. As I say, I was happy to hear the minister's announcement. But from that point on, I believe the minister would be one of the first to agree what happened amounted almost to a comedy of errors.
He announced that one million dollars would be available for this purpose in all parts of Canada. I should like hon. members to note the date-March 25, 1965. I waited some time, then I telephoned the minister's office on two occasions. I received courteous replies but I did not get a copy of the provisions or regulations governing the proposed grants. I decided I had better ask a question in the house to make it obvious to the department that it was about time these regulations were made available.
So on May 10, 1965 I asked a question in the house on this subject and the minister was kind enough to reply as follows:
We expect these details to be available for distribution in the course of the next few days.
As the hon. gentleman knows, they were not. Again, I called the mrnster's office a couple of times, receiving courteous replies but still no copies of the regulations. So on May 28, 1965 as reported at page 1771 of Hansard I again put a question to the minister.
I think at that point he was getting a little huffy, if I might use that word, just as I was. He said in reply:
I believe they are ready and are on the point of being distributed. I will now try to speed things up as much as I can.
And he did. When I called his department a day or so later, the person who answered 
me-I do not wish to give names, of course -said the minister had been raising particular "something or other", and that the regulations would be ready in a day or two. They were, indeed, and I received copies of the regulations and sent them out.
At this point I ran into another block. I do not blame the minister. I think it was probably a case of imperfect communication. There were six places in my constituency where I thought aid was needed and where it might be expected. I got in touch with those concerned, and some of them got in touch with the department and asked that a review of their facilities be made in order to determine whether the requirements were met. I believe four places were visited by officials from the department in the region, and I am afraid the people there received what they considered to be a brush-off. Again, I took the matter up with the minister, who told me that this was not the intention and that in his view further consideration should be given to the requests.
After all this, a procedure extending over a period of months, one airfield has finally been given a grant. I understand that these people, in turn, have managed to get into difficulty about it, so it is not certain whether they will, in fact, get any assistance. But this is not the responsibility of the minister, nor of his department; the grant was made available. The result is, as far as I can find out, that in the whole of Saskatchewan a total amount of, roughly, $27,000 has been made available for the purpose the minister had in mind. The town of Biggar has received $18,000 and the town of Unity has received some $9,500.
The point I wish to make is this. This plan was one which was to have been carried out throughout the whole of the dominion. Thus we might reasonably have expected that some degree of equality would be attached to the allocation of funds. I make no accusations but I th nk it is remarkable that the place which received the most funds was Despair Bay-I should, probably, say it in French, but I will not even try.
The amount received in that place was generous-I have the figure somewhere among my papers; I do not care to depend on my memory; the actual amount was sent to me by the Department of Transport at my request.

I do not seem to be able to find it in this mass of material. However, from memory, I believe this particular area received something like $250,000, give or take a few tens of thousands. The whole of Newfoundland received some $280,000-I am fairly sure that figure is correct. So, if I am anywhere near right, the province of Saskatchewan got roughly $27,000 and the province of Newfoundland got something like ten times as much.
Hon. members may say that perhaps there was more need in the province of Newfoundland. I am prepared to admit that this may be the case. The airport which received the major part of the money was located in an area where a large power development has been taking place, so there was great need for an airport there.
Nevertheless, a need also exists in the areas of Saskatchewan to which I have referred. They did not expect to receive anything like a quarter of a million dollars, but I think each airport might reasonably be expected to receive the modest amounts, in the region of $10,000 to $15,000, for which they were asking. If five or six of them had been approved it would still be far short of the large amount of money which Newfoundland received, and I would hope the minister will make a statement on this matter. I hope he will continue the policy, but that there will be a fairer distribution of the moneys he has available. I think the breakdown in communication between himself and the regional officials has been responsible for the failure of these places to get the grants, and the minister must realize that these local airports are entitled to some assistance.

I note that the railway grade crossing fund, in vote 82, was raised by $1 million last year, from $9 million to $10 million. In view of the couple of tragic accidents which occurred at intervals of almost a year in the Port Hope area, this is something to which the minister should direct his attention. There are still a large number of crossings that are far from being safe. I do not suggest that we should try to do something with crossings where the passing of trains seldom occurs, where they are out in the country with a clear view both ways; but on crossings near communities, over which there is a reasonable amount of train traffic, we should do everything we can, and spend larger sums of money in the coming year to see that they are adequately marked.

If this requires another $10 million, another $20 million or another $30 million, I think the money can be found. As a matter of fact, I have great faith in the ability of the government to find money. It has demonstrated how well it can do this under the most unfavourable circumstances, but I hope it can find it in a little more-I will not use the word legitimate-a little more open way than it did recently.
The minister has made some statements about rail line abandonment, and if I am not mistaken has supported the policy which I will be advocating. I would like him to support it openly in this house. Some railway lines are going to be taken away from areas solely because they are uneconomic. This will leave the people living in those areas in an impossible situation with respect to getting their supplies and sending out heavy, bulk materials, such as grain and other products.
It would be well nigh impossible for the provinces to face the heavy expense of putting good roads into areas where rail line abandonment has taken place. I believe the minister should make a statement saying this is something the federal government will sympathetically consider, subject to the advice of the new commissioners to be appointed under the proposed railway legislation. I know the federal government has done this in the past. It did it with regard to the Buctouche-Moncton branch line which was abandoned, or possibly not built. At that time the federal government devoted some millions of dollars to the building of a good road. As I say, I hope the minister will see fit to make a clear statement on the intentions of the government with respect to this matter.
I should now like to mention the St. Lawrence seaway. We had an emergency debate last June on the subject of the seaway, when all other business of the house was set aside. As a result of that debate I think the minister has a clear indication that the attitude of most people opposes any increase of the St. Lawrence seaway tolls. I know that what happens in the United States affects what we may do on the seaway because it operates a part of the seaway in conjunction with the Canadian authorities, the same as we operate part of it in conjunction with the American authorities. It would create a very difficult situation if we took one course in this country and the United States took another course. I understand strong arguments have been advanced in the United States favouring complete abolition of the tolls, and I believe this is what should be

November 25, 1966
Supply-Transport
finally done, because if transportation is of national importance then the seaway is also of national importance. It not only helps the western producers to move their grain to the east, and potash shipments which are likely to increase in the near future, but it also assists eastern Canadian manufacturers to send their products to the very big markets of the west.
It should not be forgotten that it is quite easy to move such things as machinery from Minneapolis to the west, bypassing the seaway altogether. If we raise the seaway tolls too high a lot of business will be diverted from eastern Canadian firms to firms in the United States which will be able to ship their products to western Canada at a lower price than that of eastern Canadian industrialists.
I can see no harm to the Atlantic provinces in whatever we may do with the St. Lawrence seaway. The only harm that would befall the maritime provinces is that they lose winter business which the port of Montreal gets, due to the fact that the lower St. Lawrence river is being kept open for much longer periods of time than used to be the case. This is a fact of life that the maritime provinces must live with; but the question of tolls does not affect them because the tolls come into operation from Montreal, inland. In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I hope the minister will make a statement on these four matters because I think they merit his attention.

Dated at Ottawa this 14th day of November, 1966.
J. R. Baldwin for Minister of Transport
Although I am aware that the minister is prohibited from giving a legal interpretation, I am sure he will be able to give an explanation in clarification of the situation, because it certainly is open to clarification. The matter I should like to raise is this: Not only did the Manseau 101 founder and sink on September 30, 1966, just below Quebec city, but the important point is that a number of persons working there lost their lives by drowning. Of the 24 persons who were on board at the time, ten drowned. I believe the technical phrase is, "missing, believed drowned". This is the wording used when the bodies are not found. I think it can be said without hesitation that they drowned.
In the letter I have just read there is no reference whatsoever to the loss of the seamen who were on board and who drowned as a result of the sinking of the Manseau 101. The heading is, "In the matter of the foundering of the dredge-" and the inquiry is, "a formal investigation into the causes which led to the foundering of the Manseau 101. Nowhere in that letter of commission is there a reference to those who lost their lives. I think this is an extremely vital and important question.
Although I do not wish to read it in its entirety, attached to this is a document headed, "Statement of the Case", which I understand will be read at the opening of the inquiry. Since this was sent to me I assume I am not transgressing any of the proprieties of the investigation if I make reference to it. The statement of the case makes reference to the fact that 10 of the 24 persons on the Manseau 101 were drowned. As one of the questions put to the inquiry, it asks how many persons were aboard the dredge and how many lost their lives. Then it goes on to make reference to lifesaving equipment, communications, periodic checks and the like. It also poses the particular question: What caused the loss of the Manseau 101?
Quite frankly I do not know whether the commissioner, Mr. Justice Noel, has authority to inquire into the cause of the loss of life. The minister nods his head, so the answer is yes. In the Canada Shipping Act, an antiquated document if ever there was one on the statute books, I see that there are a number of sections which refer to inquiries, casualties
Supply-Transport
and accidents in respect of ships. I understand that the commission of inquiry which looked into the matter of the sinking of the Huronic specifically had cognizance of the provisions of section 551 of the Canada Shipping Act which says, "A shipping casualty shall be deemed to occur-" and then there are subsections (a), (b), (c), (d), and so on. Subsection (c) reads as follows:
(c) when, by reason of any casualty happening to or on board any ship in, on or near such inland waters or coast, loss of life ensues . . .
I would think that indicates clearly that we are concerned in this commission of inquiry, and others, not only with the loss or the sinking of the ship or dredge, but that we also are concerned with and in fact should give prior thought and consideration to the matter of the loss of life. I submit that in the letter by which Mr. Justice Noel is appointed as commissioner there should be some reference to the relevant part of section 551 which deals with shipping casualties and accidents on ships. I would think that the commissioner should be asked specifically not only to inquire into what caused the foundering of the Manseau 101, but also to inquire into the cause of the loss of life.
[DOT] (12:20 p.m.)
This is vitally serious. Let me refer just briefly to the loss of the Fort William in Montreal harbour. It caught fire, capsized and sank and there was a loss of life. In spite of that loss of life, there was no direction in the terms of reference to the commission appointed to inquire into this accident to ascertain the reason for this loss of life, or to fix responsibility. As a consequence, the Canada Steamship Lines even though it was negligent in its responsibility in having a ship built that was not seaworthy because of the ballast tanks and in not having a sufficient number of people on watch, was relieved of any responsibility because the commission did not have the authority to inquire into this loss of life.
That is perhaps also the case to which I first referred. Mr. Justice Noel was appointed to look into only the causes which led to the foundering of the Manseau 101, but he will not be in a position to make any inquiry into the loss of ten lives. Nor will he have any authority to place the responsibility on anyone's shoulders.
Section 558 of the Canada Shipping Act makes reference to formal inquiries which can be made and covers the situation quite extensively. When an accident occurs and there is a

November 25, 1966
Supply-Transport
loss of life or injuries are inflicted upon seamen, an inquiry should be made not only as to the causes of the accident, but as to the responsibility and where it should rest. We must think in terms of preventing similar accidents from happening in the future, and we can do this best by inquiring into causes of accidents and responsibility for loss of life. We can then make regulations based on our experience.
All our safety regulations in industry have been based on our experience, and the realization that certain companies had done certain unsafe things. As a consequence, to ensure the safety of their employees, regulations were passed to restrict those companies from carrying out such unsafe actions. I am sure the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Transport, having been a hard-rock miner, knows how various safety regulations were founded on experience. As a result of coming from his part of the country, I am sure he knows about the coal mining industry when horses were used underground. He must be aware of the fact that when an accident occurred in those days the foreman, superintendent or the man in control of things at the mine was more interested in saving the horses than in saving the employees. There was a pretty good reason for that attitude: It was that horses cost money, but employees came free.
Those are the kinds of things which existed in the early days, but because of public demand and the conscientious approach of politicans safety regulations have been devised. We must draw upon our experience in the shipping industry to promulgate regulations for the safe operation of ships in order so far as possible to protect the sailors who work on those ships. We must cut down these accidents as much as possible, so that lives are not lost as the result of unsafe acts or carelessness.
For these reasons it is vitally important, in this case as in others that the commission be given the authority to inquire into not only the causes of the accident but the reasons for the loss of life. It must also have the authority to fix responsibility for that loss of life.
We must keep in mind those who are now widows and orphans because of the loss of these ten sailors in the Manseau 101 accident. Compensation in terms of money must be paid to the survivors because that is the only way compensation can be made. We cannot bring back to life individuals who were killed. Society must compel those who are

responsible to meet in some way or other their obligation to accept responsibility for the loss of life, and to contribute to the economic welfare of the widows and orphans left behind.
On the basis of compensation legislation throughout this nation, pensions are paid to widows and orphans of individuals who have lost their lives while on the job. For this reason we must have formal inquiries into these accidents and into the reasons for the loss of life. These inquiries must fix responsibility. There have been conflicts in the application of the provisions of the Canada Shipping Act and the various compensation acts of the provinces. I do not know whether these conflicts have ever been resolved, but I know they did exist. On the west coast, so far as fishing vessels are concerned, the compensation board is precluded from engaging in any safety inspection because this matter comes under the Canada Shipping Act and the federal authority.
It is my understanding that the federal government does not engage very extensively in accident prevention inspection programs, but leaves this to steamship inspection regulations. I also understand that the federal government concerns itself only to a minor degree with safety factors and working conditions of employees on the ships.
I leave the subject there, in the hope that the minister will realize the vital importance that must be attached to the loss of life, and will give some clear, concise and full explanation not only as to what he intends to do in respect of the Manseau 101, but in respect of future accidents as well.
Are you referring to the new minister?

I do not care whether it is the old minister, the new minister or the future minister, but someone should make a statement of policy in this regard.
[DOT] (12:30 p.m.)

Mr. Chairman, I wish to take advantage of the consideration of the estimates of the Department of Transport to call the minister's attention to some faults in the line which is of interest to us, that is the Montreal-Chambord and Chambord-Dolbeau line.
Allow me first to recognize the good work done by the minister in previous years when I would go to his office to plead for the Saguenay-Lake St. John railway. I think that,
November 25, 1966

thanks to his repeated representations to the C.N.R., we succeeded at least in keeping what we already had, namely our C.N.R. stations. As a matter of fact, when practically a third of our stations were stated for closing, we succeeded in keeping them for at least a few years. I feel that the minister is to be thanked for that and I wish to congratulate him.
Also we succeeded in keeping our passenger coach from Chambord to Dolbeau and I feel that if the minister had not intervened in time, when the people in Quebec wanted to abolish that section of the passenger service and provide us with a bus service, that part of the service would have been abolished.
I think that the people in the area are very satisfied and the minister will realize that we were right at that time and the years to come will show him that we were right in wanting to keep that passenger coach, because of the tidy income which our region brings to the C.N.R. in freight traffic. That was shown to him by the financial reports of companies such as Domtar, Gagnon & Freres, and five or six other industries which use the C.N.R. service.
I wish to point out also that the minister was very effective about the restaurant in Chambord, which had been closed definitely, although it is a transit point for the two regions. After getting in touch with the C.N.R. authorities, the minister secured the immediate re-opening of that restaurant to the great satisfaction of the people throughout the region.
I think that something was done also with regard to safety; there is still much to be done and I am sure that the minister is aware of it. There is no need to mention all those things one by one, but I simply want to say it in passing to keep from being accused of criticizing only and to prove that we keep our eyes open and see what a minister does in our region.
I would like to deal with another matter, and that is the quality of ordinary coaches. I simply want to call the attention of the minister to that because we had-and I like to say it-for about a year or a year and a half a very clean coach which the personnel tried very hard to keep clean, to such an extent that in our area one is not even allowed to put one's feet on the seat. As soon as a woman would put her feet on a seat, the man in charge would come and very politely give her a piece of paper to put under her feet.
We kept that car somewhat like the apple of our eye. It was the cleanest car in the area.
Supply-Transport
Now, about a month ago, they simply took it away and replaced it with a loathsome, dirty, torn-up and soiled car. I think it is a car which had been scrapped in Montreal and which was subsequently sent to our area.
Let the minister be assured that it is no encouragement for the staff who endeavoured to keep that car perfectly clean. Therefore, I ask the minister to make representations with C.N.R. authorities, to obtain, not other people's cars, but rather our own car that our people, our authorities, the C.N.R. staff made efforts to keep incomparably clean. The people of our area would be very grateful if it came back immediately and if they had the car which served them for almost one year.
The same holds true for sleeping cars. I think there is a lot of room for improvement in this regard because, without saying that the one we now have is good only for scrapping, I would say it is not doing its job of transporting people-

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Human persons.

-human persons.
I believe the minister should point out to persons responsible-some cleaning up can be done, we can see very clean cars on other lines, like Quebec-Montreal, Quebec-Ottawa, Quebec-Toronto-the fact that people in our area are not more stupid than elsewhere and are simply asking to be served the way other people are.
As regards the staff, sir, we are generally satisfied at present with those mainly responsible, although there still exist some abuses. As we say, they still put one over on us from time to time, by placing in our cars people who cannot speak French. On my last trip, and this may surprise the hon. minister, there was a person in charge of the train, a young man, who had been hired recently and who could not even speak one word of French. The population in our area is 98 per cent French. This may be an oversight on the part of Canadian National authorities, but I think such a mistake should not be repeated and the minister should make sure that bilingual people are hired, at least in our area.
As regards the other question-I do not intend to deal at length with this subject, as we have only three hours at our disposal and I would like my colleagues to have the opportunity to say a few words-I am referring to the cost of berths in sleeping cars, I think we should bring this little trick to the attention of parliament. I say it is a little trick, because when we reserved a berth some time ago, we

November 25, 1966
S upp ly-Transport
used to pay $4.50, $5 and now we have to pay $9 and we are told that the meal is included in the price of the berth.
Now, Mr. Chairman, as a matter of fact, no meals are served in my area. We get aboard the train at Chambord at ten o'clock, half past ten, and at Chambord or Dolbeau we pay the price of the berth and meal and we arrive in Montreal at seven o'clock in the morning. The dining car opens at eight o'clock. The last time, I had to rush at a quarter to 7 and I finally got a cup of coffee. It seems it was the last one, since about ten people came after me and were told that there was no more coffee.
I believe that an increase of $3.50 for a cup of coffee that we never get is a little trick that is unpardonable.
The people are complaining, and I think they are justified in doing so. Once again, I call the minister's attention to this point. If meals cannot be served-anyway, it is too early to serve breakfast, since we reach Montreal at seven o'clock, or at 10 minutes to 7-let them reduce the price of the ticket instead of including these famous meals which are never served in the price of a sleeping-car ticket.
Finally, since winter is coming, I should like to say a word about locomotives. Hon. members will remember that I made a speech about these locomotives last year. I went to see the minister in his office and, since it was almost spring, we agreed that the same locomotive should be kept.
The locomotive used in the summer cannot logically and safely be used in winter on account of our climate and the amount of snowfall. As soon as there is a little snow storm, the small locomotive we have at present has no visibility. I talked about my own experiences last year. I was not talking through my hat, and there have also been complaints from the authorities saying that the engineer could go on for ten or twenty miles without seeing anything at all, not even railway crossings. Since we have locomotives made for this climate which go up to Chibougamau, it would be quite easy to give us a similar engine.
I hope this is enough to bring this point to the attention of the minister. I speak about this rather early in the year, because there is no snow yet, and if the Canadian National cannot give us the locomotive we want all year round, let them use it during the worst three or four winter months and go back to the old locomotive in the summer.
Once more, I am confident that the minister is concerning himself with our area this year. Unfortunately, some local newspapers have

stated that we are doing nothing, that the Canadian National equipment is completely dilapidated and that there is no service. Well, no. We should not make things worse than they are. I believe that something has been accomplished; however, a lot remains to be done, and I would ask the minister to kindly call the attention of the Canadian National authorities to the situation, so that they may improve our railway system.

Mr. Chairman, before item 1 of the minister's estimates is passed I wish to make reference to a few points which will be largely of interest to people interested in the Vancouver harbour. I think the recent announcement of the minister when he was in Vancouver that the boundaries of the harbour of Vancouver would be extended southward along the coast to the 49th parallel of the United States boundary was a welcome piece of news for all those who are interested in the welfare of Vancouver harbour. This simply means that the department is following the policy of the authority on local development, so that as the harbour grows, and develops its capacity for the handling of bulk commodities, the jurisdiction of the National Harbours Board will be there in advance of that development. There has been considerable talk in Vancouver and in the whole of British Columbia that enormous bulk loading facilities will be built on the coast between the inside harbour of Vancouver and the 49th parallel south of Vancouver harbour. This simply means that facilities will be developed there, perhaps by the province of British Columbia itself. This has given rise to much speculation as to just where the jurisdiction for harbour facilities lies.
Of course the jurisdiction lies with the National Harbours Board, and the minister's announcement cleared up that matter for anyone who is interested. It in no way hampers the development, either by British Columbia or by private interests, of harbour facilities within the jurisdiction of the National Harbours Board, because I am sure the minister and his department would welcome those developments; but it does make it very certain for all time as to where the jurisdiction lies. This is a considerable step forward.
The day may come, and none too soon, when Vancouver might be the site of harbour berths capable of handling the super vessels which are now being built, largely in Japan for the handling of bulk commodities. These
November 25, 1966

vessels range in size from 100,000 to 200,000 tons and sometimes exceed even that tonnage. These are one-purpose vessels which move from one berth on one side of the ocean to another berth on another side. They are specifically prepared for that purpose and they move perhaps only one or two commodities between the two berths that are prepared for them. If such developments come, and I hope they will, they will in no way reflect upon the capability of the inner harbour of Vancouver to handle an ever increasing volume of tonnage and indeed to handle much larger vessels than are now entering that harbour.
It was also very welcome news to learn that the National Harbours Board had acquired within the inner harbour the long disputed C.P.R. lands, because this will enable the board to expand greatly its interest in the harbour of Vancouver. As I have said in the house before, the harbour of Vancouver is the only one of the major National Harbours Board ports which is not wholly or almost wholly owned by the federal government and under development by it, so that the additional acquisition of lands from the C.P.R. in the area of the best deep-water berths in Vancouver harbour is very welcome. It presages further development, such as we have seen in the National Harbours Board owned wharves on the harbour, which are the best facilities we have in the harbour of Vancouver. I hope that before the estimates are passed the minister may be able to give us a summary of the proposals for the development of the lands which have been acquired from the C.P.R.
It was also welcome news that grain handling facilities are improving, although I think anyone who has taken any interest in the development of grain handling out of the port of Vancouver during the last few years would probably want to say that it is not enough. However it is certainly very encouraging to see that, for example, some jetties have been extended to a length of 750 feet to accommodate the very long vessels which are now loading at grain elevators in the port of Vancouver. Formerly these vessels could only load through some of their holds, because the jetties were not long enough for vessels of that dimension. Consequently the quick loading of these vessels and their capability of turning around quickly was impeded by the limited equipment of the harbour.
We were very glad to see the development of the elevator on the north shore of the
Supply-Transport
harbour and to note that engineering is undei way for the construction of a C.N.R. bridge, which will be close to and parallel with the Second Narrows bridge, to bring another rail line or a series of them to the north shore, because the north shore of Vancouver harbour is developing into a very important bulk and grain loading terminal.
I think all these developments around the harbour of Vancouver must eventually mean that this harbour will have to acquire some kind of harbour railway so that interswitching from the north to the south shore and the movement of cars in the lower mainland will be under a co-ordinated single authority.
[DOT] (12:50 p.m.)
Five railways enter the lower mainland, the old B.C. Electric Railway, the Great Northern Railway, the Canadian National Railways, the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Pacific Great Eastern. Those five railways, switching cars among one another often with great delay, face a great problem in the movement of commodities and in the efficient handling of commodities on the lower mainland. Certainly we would handle grain more efficiently if we had a major joint yard, handling cars in the grain trade and moving them efficiently to the harbour elevators. Suggestions along these lines have been made many times. That would require bringing together the several railways which serve the lower mainland and organizing them perhaps into a union company. This could be brought about, in time, by the intervention of the crown, the Minister of Transport, or some agency of the minister which would encourage such development, and thereby bring about the orderly handling of commodities on the lower mainland of British Columbia. In that port the dry tonnage of goods shipped and handled this year will far exceed the dry tonnage handled in any other port in Canada. For the development of the port we shall need assistance, to allow its expansion.
I want to talk a little about pollution and debris in the harbour. Over the years this has been increasing, and it is something which various agencies of the Department of Transport, which are responsible for this, have dealt with and attempted to suppress. It is evident to anybody looking at the harbour, and seeing the quantities of floating chips, bark, logs, oil and junk that wash back and forth in the harbour, as well as outside in English Bay, thus spoiling properties and boats, and fouling propellers of pleasure craft, that the job of controlling debris in our major

November 25, 1966
S upp ly-Transport
harbours, and particularly in the great harbour I refer to, is not being done well enough. Debris is not under control.
What is being done by the federal government to step up debris control? I ask this because it is absolutely shocking-and 1 think I speak for members on both sides of the house interested in that great harbour-to see that debris. I say something must be done. And more must be done than has been done, whatever have been the efforts of the federal government or other agencies, if we are to control the pollution and debris washing back and forth in Vancouver harbour.
I pass on now to mention briefly another problem which came to my desk recently, through corresponding with businessmen in the city of Vancouver. I refer to air service to the prairies. What is happening is this: The air services which comprise our major airlines, and which serve western Canada, are centered in eastern Canada. I presume that those heading Air Canada tend to look on eastern Canada as the centre of the universe, and to regard air transport as stemming from that great centre. But the west coast is developing into a great metropolitan area, and more and more the city of Vancouver is serving the interior of the continent and the prairies particularly with all kinds of services. Businessmen increasingly are moving back and forth between the coast and the prairies.
Businessmen tell me that it is difficult to arrange air trips enabling them to move efficiently to the prairies and back to the coast, without losing valuable time. I know that those looking into the matter have been in touch with the minister, with the air lines and with the mayors and chambers of commerce on the prairie to see what can be done.
I do not think the matter is being looked into by Air Canada as effectively as it ought to be and I urge the minister to take the matter in hand, to get hold of Mr. McGregor, and ask him if indeed the whole universe is to be served out of eastern Canada, or if he could look at other growing centres in Canada, and the growing air traffic developing there, and originate more flights to the prairies which will be effective in helping western businessmen.
I will not say any more on the estimates now, except that for the Department of Transport, in its work on the west coast, I believe the year has been an effective one. But I would not want the minister to feel that the west coast is developing so slowly that the pace of the department is sufficient to keep up with it. I urge the minister to keep an eye on

what we are doing. We shall need his ever increasing services.

The hon. member for Kin-dersley, Mr. Chairman, dealt in his speech with the points I had intended to bring up, so that I will not repeat what has been said. But I do wish to refer particularly, as he referred, to possible assistance for local airstrips. I hope the minister will agree to the request for more information about this assistance. We want to know where these airstrips are now, and I suspect Saskatchewan has been neglected very much in this regard.
Several communities in Moose Jaw-Lake Centre are interested in developing local airstrips, particularly because of the potential in the potash industry. I refer specifically to the area of Watrous. At the request of the mayor and local officials of Watrous I secured all the information I could about assistance to local airstrips, and I passed that information on. According to reports I received, there was so much red tape that they finally proceeded on their own, and they built a fairly good airstrip through their own efforts. I do not criticize the department too much, but I think it could make it easier for communities to develop their local airstrips. I ask again that the minister deal with this matter when he replies. I do not think sufficient assistance has been given to airstrips. Four or five other areas in my constituency are interested in some form of air service to help develop the potash industry.
About the rail crossing fund, seaway tolls, rail line abandonment and passenger service I shall not say anything at this time, but I give the minister fair warning that when Bill No. C-231 comes up for clause by clause study, those matters affecting the establishment of the Canadian Transportation Commission will be brought up and talked about to considerable length. I intend to take part in the debate on that measure.
[DOT] (1:00 p.m.)
The proposal I wish to make now does not wholly affect the Department of Transport, but the department is involved. It is concerned with the relocation of an airport. Before I go further, let me say that I am in complete agreement with what was said by the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra about the need for improved air services on the prairies.
I represent the city of Moose Jaw and a very large part of the city of Regina. The proposal I wish to put forward now has been advanced by officials in Regina, and it relates
November 25. 1966

to the possibility of establishing an industrial corridor between Moose Jaw and Regina. This aspect does not directly concern the Department of Transport, but there is a part of it which does. The proposal would involve the relocation of the airport half way between Moose Jaw and Regina as part of a scheme to encourage industries to establish themselves between Moose Jaw and Regina where all the necessary conditions for industrial development exist, including highways, railways, gas, water and power services. What it is hoped to establish is something along the lines of the industrial corridor between Toronto and Hamilton.
The present airport is within the city of Regina. I say this advisedly, because on two sides residential homes have been built right up to the perimeter and there is little possibility of the runways being used by large jet planes when these are brought into service in the future. As I have suggested, this idea is not my own entirely; it has been advanced by prominent officials in both Regina and Moose Jaw. The idea would be to relocate the airport half way between the two cities. Moose Jaw is not at present served by an air service and the people of that city are disturbed about having to travel to Regina, 42 miles away, to board a plane for passenger travel.
The proposal which I have briefly outlined has been advanced, as I say, by both cities and I draw it to the minister's attention mainly to let him know that in my opinion it is a feasible idea and one which should be considered very carefully before any further expansion takes place at Regina airfield. Future capital investment there would, of course, make it more difficult to relocate.
I venture to say that the minister will be hearing a great deal more about this subject. I shall be speaking about it. He will also be hearing from officials in Regina and Moose Jaw earlier now, perhaps, than might otherwise have been the case. Speaking on my own responsibility, let me say that in my opinion the idea is a very good one and I hope the minister will look at it closely when he is considering further development in the area. As Minister of Transport, he will no doubt be interested to know that a four-lane highway is being built between Moose Jaw and Regina and that within the next few days 25 miles of the 42 miles of road will be open to traffic, if they are not already open. I see great prospects for this area, and, for the moment, I leave this matter for the minister's consideration.

There are, of course a number of matters which are of vital interest to me and to my constituents in connection with the estimates of the Department of Transport which are now before us.
The problem of passenger train service has not been resolved completely to our satisfaction. However, the C.P.R. aspect has been referred to a committee, so I shall not discuss that subject, now. Then again, all the new proposals in Bill C-231 are of vital concern to the area of Canada which I represent, but I will refrain from discussing any part of what is contained in that measure until it is returned to the house.
I wish to speak briefly, today, about two matters which are not under active consideration by any other committee of this house. The first concerns the transport of grain from the wheat growing areas of Canada into export position. I am pleased to see the Minister of Finance here because I know he is familiar with this subject.
I have raised this question on the orders of the day. I have placed it before the Minister of Trade and Commerce who is now responsible to parliament for the Canadian wheat board. Every time I bring it up, no matter which minister replies, I am always told that the movement of grain out of the prairies to export position is progressing in a highly satisfactory way; that the volume dealt with is greater than last year; that we should be very pleased, and so on. I am not disagreeing with this. I want to commend the Minister of Transport, the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the railroads on the job they have done from March 30 to the end of July for the last crop year, and during this crop year as far as total volume is concerned.
Nevertheless, there is another problem. No matter how highly one can commend all those concerned on the total volume moved, there is still the wide disparity which exists between quotas at points which are, after all, very close together. One cannot make the argument that the total volume transported is high when one point is on a quota of one bushel per acre and another, 50 miles away, is on a four bushel quota.
My plea today is that something should be done to remedy such inequities. I am not proposing that the government should set up a transport controller with full power to direct the railways. But it seems to me that if justice is to be done we should see to it, perhaps by way of a co-ordinating committee, that these

November 25, 1966
Supply-Transport
disparities do not continue to arise every year as is the case in my riding. I wish to make this very clear: I am not questioning the total volume moved. I am questioning the way in which box cars or grain cars are allocated to the various points, and I am asking that each farmer should have reasonably equitable access to the market in the months between September and December. We know that by the end of the crop year these quotas are usually evened out. I can appreciated that there is good and sound reason why they cannot be completely even throughout the shipping season. My difficulty is that they get too far apart. Why should one point be on a four bushel quota while another only 15 miles away is on a one bushel quota? That is too much for farmers to understand.
I am making no criticism of the Canadian Wheat Board. As I understand it, the wheat board has no authority to order railroads to put cars at certain points.
[DOT] (1:10 p.m.)
In addition to that, Mr. Chairman, the Canadian Wheat Board can only open the quota at a specific shipping point if and when there is space, and the only way to get space at a shipping point is for the railways to put cars there to haul out some grain. This is not a criticism of the wheat board. I am sure it opens the quotas as quickly as the space permits, but it has no power except by way of suggestion, to see that a point that is very low so far as quota is concerned is given extra consideration. This is a problem, and the question is what to do about it.
I am not suggesting that we give some traffic or freight co-ordinator full authority to direct the railways to do this, but I think that the co-ordinating committee which the Minister of Finance set up, I believe in the fall of 1965, served a useful purpose. There were representatives on it from the terminal elevators, the railways, the wheat board, and some of the co-operative or line terminals. Following the announcement of the setting up of that committee, the situation improved.
On November 16, in answer to a question of mine, the Minister of Transport, as recorded at page 9958 of Hansard, said:
I think the arrangements which are in existence at the present time are less formal than they were last year.
I was referring to the co-ordinating committee. If that committee could serve a useful purpose in providing more uniform quotas, I would urge the minister to set it up again to examine the difference in quotas at various

points and see if it could convince the railways that they would serve the whole area better by concentrating the allocation of cars at some points with very low quotas. I make that plea to the Minister of Finance and to the Minister of Transport, and I am sure they will try to do something about it.
The question of air services on the prairies has been raised by a number of hon. members. The Minister of Transport knows I have asked him a number of times when we are going to get some regular scheduled air service into Medicine Hat. The minister will recall that it was a long, difficult battle, or at least that it took a series of negotiations to get the Department of Transport to improve the runway at Medicine Hat. That runway was built for a wartime training base and could not take care of aircraft larger than a DC-3. As a matter of fact, once or twice even a DC-3 went through it. But now we have a new runway. We have had it for two or three years, but we have no air service to make use of it.
I plead with the minister to use his very persuasive influence on Air Canada to give some consideration to providing a regular service into Medicine Hat, and from Medicine Hat to Calgary and Edmonton. Particularly connections should be provided with the trans-continental runs from Calgary to Vancouver, and from Calgary to Winnipeg, Toronto, and eastwards.
If the minister is unable to convince Air Canada to do this, then my alternative plea is that he try to make an arrangement between Air Canada and the regional carriers whereby passengers can buy tickets from Medicine Hat to Toronto or to Vancouver, depending on which direction they are travelling. I am not going to talk about Red Deer, even though it has no airport, because it is 100 miles closer to air service, but I would point out that a one way economy ticket from Edmonton to Ottawa costs $96. But from Medicine Hat, which is closer to Ottawa, a passenger has to pay $16 more to get to Calgary, and in the process has to buy two tickets.
The small regional carrier operating there is to a large degree acting as a feeder line for Air Canada, and some consideration should be given to providing a single ticket from Medicine Hat for runs west, northwest or east from Calgary. Under the new regional air policy, there should be a regulation under which one can buy a ticket from any point in Canada to any other point in Canada, a ticket that will be honoured by all air lines. This is
November 25, 1966

already done by agreement in the international field, and surely it there can be such an agreement among international carriers it should be possible to have a similar agreement within Canada.
I would also like to ask the minister how we are getting along with the new regional air policy. Have there been many applications made under it? I would like to know if the air line now serving Medicine Hat, and other air lines serving other areas in Alberta, have applied for the benefits, or whatever one wants to call them, provided by this new policy. If they have not, then would the minister explain to the committee, so that the country and the air lines may know, the procedure they should follow to avail themselves of this new policy?
In closing, Mr. Chairman, I just say that a city of 30,000 people is large enough to warrant some air service. It is far enough away from other major cities to have its own service. In many respects air service is the most convenient form of passenger traffic for it. We have been waiting for several years to be provided with a satisfactory service connecting with the other major cities in western Canada, and particularly with transcontinental runs. I hope some positive action is soon taken so that we do not have to go on waiting and waiting. The new regional air policy is a step in the right direction, but we would like to see better effects from it in the city of Medicine Hat and the surrounding district.

On behalf of the constituency which I have the honour to represent, I want to protest most emphatically against the treatment given by the Canadian National Railways, to its population and especially to those residing in that part of the riding between Kapuskasing and Hearst. The transcontinental railway line was begun with the hope that it would open up a new country, and in effect it did. From the start of service on the transcontinental line up until 1932 the district from Cochrane to Hearst, all of the western district of the province of Quebec and the northeastern district of the province of Ontario, enjoyed the services of train No. 1 and train No. 2 travelling between Quebec and Winnipeg. But in 1932 this service was discontinued and these trains have been operating on the line between Ottawa, North Bay and Winnipeg.
When that service was removed, a Budd car was provided from Cochrane to Hearst. After making many representations to the C.N.R., it finally decided to give us a train with a steam
Supply-Transport
locomotive, an express car and a passenger coach.
[DOT] (1:20 p.m.)
In the late 1950's I remember very well writing to the president of the C.N.R. to ask him whether this was not one of the first coaches the C.N.R. had ever used on its line. It was a wooden car, heated with a coal furnace. It was not fit for human beings. Finally in 1962, with the help of public bodies such as municipal councils, boards of trade and chambers of commerce, we convinced the C.N.R. that a good train service between Toronto and Hearst was needed. In the month of October, 1962, we were provided with a direct train service from Toronto to Hearst and vice versa. Then, in 1965, the C.N.R. made an application to the Board of Transport Commissioners asking that the service between Kapuskasing and Hearst be discontinued. At this point, I should like to thank the minister for the assistance he gave in this matter. The Board of Transport Commissioners agreed to hold hearings in the district to receive the brief protesting curtailment of that train service. Sittings were held at Hearst and Kapuskasing. In April representatives held a sitting at Hearst and Kapuskasing. In June one was held at Kapuskasing. At both sittings briefs were presented by the chambers of commerce, the municipal councils and other business interests. The point which is of interest to me is that whenever a brief was to be presented at those sittings, a copy of it had to be sent beforehand to the C.N.R. This enabled the C.N.R. lawyer to prepare his defence in such a way that we would not be able to answer it successfully.
It is very easy to juggle figures. As a result of juggling figures the C.N.R. managed to convince the board the service ought to be discontinued and replaced by a bus service. I, Mr. Chairman, am one who thinks the time has come when commissions and boards have too much authority compared to the person who is elected to serve the people he represents.
Hear, hear.

I was greatly disappointed indeed when I was informed by the Board of Transport Commissioners that it had agreed to give the C.N.R. permission to curtail that train service.
At this point I should like to mention that in the district I represent, because of the great industrialization and the wages paid, the people in this area are among those groups who are contributing to the national revenue of

November 25, 1966
Supply-Transport
this country to the greatest extent. I hesitate to say this, but I believe the people of my district are among those who pay the highest rate of income tax. It seems to me, in a region such as this where the potential is so great and where the rate of development in the future is going to increase rather than decrease, the C.N.R. should reconsider their argument in respect of the differentiation between freight service and passenger service revenues. They tell us that although they might be making good money from the freight business, they are losing on the passenger service.
If there were no people to operate the industries in this area, and if there were no people living there, there would be no freight to ship. So, in all fairness, it seems to me that the C.N.R. should consider both sides of the story and give consideration to the needs of the people in this district from which the company obtains a good deal of its freight revenue. They should give more consideration than they appear to have given in the past. Just a few days ago I had a phone call from Hearst. The C.N.R., which had promised to give the best possible service by buses, now has advised the municipal council of the town of Hearst that only the hand luggage will be transported on those buses. In fact any other baggage will have to be shipped at the expense of the passenger. He will have to pay the transportation from Hearst to Kapus-kasing, and vice versa. At Kapuskasing, where they had promised they would continue the very good service we had since 1962, already they have replaced the pullman car with one which has compartments and roomettes only. There are no berths in this pullman car. I have a letter from the municipal council of the town of Kapuskasing stating that because this pullman car has been changed, the fare from Kapuskasing to Toronto has been increased by $11.
If this is the way the C.N.R. is going to treat the population in northern Ontario, then I believe it is time they should tell us they want to do away with all passenger service; then we would know where we stand. It would not surprise me if, in the back of their minds, they have the intention of decreasing rather than increasing the passenger service so that they would be justified in applying to the Board of Transport Commissioners for the discontinuation of the service between Por-quis Junction and Kapuskasing. Then, we would be left with no service at all.
[Mr. Habel.l
Mr. Chairman, I know that the Minister of Transport has shown an interest in the northern part of the province, but it seems to me with	the	authority	given to these
boards-whether it be the Board of Transport Commissioners, the Air Transport Board or others-we seem to be forgetting the people who are elected to represent their constituents. I must say quite frankly that I even hesitated to take part in this debate. I am not ashamed to say I have reached the point where I have asked myself whether it is worth putting our case before the government which might be well intentioned but is blocked by those boards and commissions which have more authority than the government itself. I also could have mentioned the situation in respect of freight rates. I have had many complaints about the high freight rates which are applicable in northern Ontario.
[DOT] (1:30 p.m.)
These high freight rates apply particularly to the Kapuskasing and Cochrane areas. Let me give you an example of the result. We can purchase gasoline here in Ottawa for 39.8 cents a gallon but in Cochrane and Kapuskasing we must pay 54 to 56 cents a gallon. I could also use the example of the lumber industry in our area. These companies have to compete with companies in other districts, yet they have a hard time convincing the C.N.R. that they must have lower rates in order to keep this industry running full time. They often have trouble in obtaining a reasonable rate to ship the wood chips which result from their operations.
Let me also refer to problems in respect of the maintenance of stations. At Smooth Rock Falls there is a large pulp and paper mill which added a $14 million extension about a year ago. The station happens to be located two and a half miles from the town. There is no service whatever at that station on Saturday and Sunday. There is not even a telephone that can be used by passengers to call a taxi. The local chamber of commerce has worked hard to solve this problem. They have met with representatives of the C.N.R. and I have written many letters about it.
I have taken this opportunity to let the minister and the Department of Transport know about our feelings. In conclusion, I protest strongly on behalf of those I represent because of these problems. All we are asking is to be treated as Canadians on an equal basis with Canadians in other parts of this country.
