Would the hon. member answer a question?
Yes.

First, I should like to commend him tor rallying against the C.N.R. in respect of having removed the main line, such as it was, from that part of Ontario. Will he fight with equal fervour against the government relocating the main line of trans-Canada pipe lines from that same area?

As far as the trans-Canada pipe line is concerned, and I am glad the hon. member asked me this question, I must say in all frankness that I do not belong to that party which takes pleasure in trying to draw blood out of wounds.

Mr. Chairman, I welcome this opportunity to make a few brief remarks during our consideration of item No. 1 of the estimates of the Department of Transport. I realize there is a time limit, so my remarks will be brief.
I feel duty-bound, because I am a member of the standing committee of this house on transport and communications, to make a few references to problems pertaining to transportation in Canada. I am sure the members of this house, and the public in general, realize that this standing committee has devoted most of its time during the last couple of months to hearing briefs presented by numerous individuals and organizations regarding Bill No. C-231 based on the MacPherson royal commission report. Like the hon. member for Medicine Hat, I am not going to refer to this bill in detail because there is a time and place for everything, but I look forward to the discussion of this matter when it comes before the house.
Yesterday I was very impressed by the evidence given by Dr. Ernest W. Williams, Jr., professor of transport, and Dr. George H. Borts. They strongly suggested that before the provisions of Bill C-231 are Anally put into effect the minister should consider several suggestions presented to that committee by those two competent gentlemen.
The hon. member for Medicine Hat also referred to something of great importance to people in western Canada, particularly those in farming areas; that is, the movement of grain to marketable positions. He referred at some length to the allocation of boxcars, but there is one other factor in this regard to which consideration should be given.
Supply-Transport
The railway companies must be aware of the fact that boxcars used for handling grain have become obsolete. The same boxcars have been used for the last 20, 30 or even a greater number of years with very little change in technological development. The roadbeds of today are of such a character that much heavier loads can be carried.
Boxcars used for the handling of grain have a capacity of some 2,000 to 3,000 bushels. When we consider what has been done with regard to the transportation of minerals, we And that very modern techniques have been adopted. I do not understand why the railway companies have overlooked the possibility of improving boxcars for handling grain. These boxcars could be enlarged to a capacity of between 5,000, 6,000 or perhaps even 10,000 bushels. They could be designed with hopper bottoms and collapsible tops that could be opened to facilitate loading. With the increased capacity and the more efficient design, the cost of handling grain would be less and the efficiency would be greater. Perhaps this could be taken into consideration by members of the standing committee when it is drafting its recommendations to the department.
A previous speaker referred to airport renovation and assistance by the Department of Transport to various municipal and secondary airports. I agree with his remarks, and I have in mind those areas in Canada where airports were built during wartime in conjunction with our air training program. A number of these have been turned over to municipal bodies for maintenance and use by local Aying clubs. The airport at the city of Estevan falls into this category, but the municipal officials have been waiting with great patience for years for the government to make up its mind what assistance it is going to give for the maintenance and renovation of this airport. Many of these airports are of vital concern to local areas. They could be of importance to our national defence effort at some future date. Vast amounts of money were spent in developing them, and I think it would be a wilful waste if the government were not to expedite its assistance to these various municipalities.
I should like to refer in passing to rail line abandonments. I have on the order paper, under item 48, Bill C-86 which deals with a moratorium in respect of rail line abandonments. In all fairness I must say that I am pleased, as I think most western Canadians are, with the action the government took prior to the passage of Bill C-231, to provide a

November 25, 1966
Supply-Transport
moratorium in respect of rail line abandonments. This has eased the tension and concern which has been expressed in many areas in the last several years regarding the wholesale abandonment of rail lines.
[DOT] (1:40 p.m.)
Naturally, we will go into the question of policy when dealing with the legislation under Bill C-231. There will be considerable opposition in certain areas to the proposed abandonments, but by and large this policy has been a step forward. I come from an area which had a great deal of experience in the matter of rail line abandonment before the MacPherson commission made its report. I am pleased that the goverment has taken this action. I hope that in some small measure I was able to contribute to the decision, because I put enough statements and comments on the record of the House of Commons, regarding this problem as members of the transportation committee will know.
The hon. member for Kindersley has spoken at some length on the question of tolls on the St. Lawrence seaway. I hope the government will soon make a final decision in this respect and will allay the fears that are still in the minds of many western Canadians with respect to increasing these tolls. I think this is an area in which the decision should be made as soon as possible. This question does not only affect people in western Canada but those adjacent to the St. Lawrence seaway and others using that great waterway.
I should like to make a few remarks regarding passenger services on the railways. We are approaching the Yuletide season. I recently had experience in trying to obtain reservations on the railway. I found the railways are having difficulty in meeting requests for passenger reservations. There still seems to be a hesitancy on the part of the C.P.R. to introduce an efficient reservation system and provide services that are acceptable to the people.
I was naturally quite concerned to learn of the difficulties experienced in this field. I had the privilege, as a member of the transportation committee, of travelling with the committee when it made a survey of passenger services last May. At that time we travelled from Vancouver east to Fort William and listened to the representations of many citizens of Canada with respect to these services. I was disappointed when the railroad decided in complying with the committee's request to reinstate at least a partial service for our centennial year, they did not come back to the

original title of that train and call it "The Dominion" rather than "Expo '67". This leaves the impression they are providing the service only temporarily, and are still determined to discontinue it after the centennial year. I believe there is a great deal of support for the retention of this service, not only from the people of western Canada but Canadians all across this country. They want adequate passenger rail service provided for those people who wish to use that service rather than air service.
I was interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra with respect to the schedules of Air Canada. The hon. member for Saskatoon and myself had this problem brought to our attention by letter. We brought it to the attention of the government on several occasions by asking questions in the house. I had the pleasure of discussing the matter with the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra, because the complaint originated in his riding. He and I agreed that something should be done. I suggested to the hon. member at that time that he was the man most responsible for raising this question because people in his area were making the complaints.
I think there has been too great a tendency on the part of Air Canada to concentrate their services in eastern Canada, the larger centres in this country and the most heavily populated points. In this connection, I remember the debates in the house with respect to the removal of the aircraft servicing facilities from Winnipeg to Montreal. There has been too great a tendency to ignore western Canada when originating services and schedules. One man told me that he could get from Vancouver to Mexico City faster than he could get from there to Regina or Saskatoon. I believe Mr. McGregor should be admonished into taking a serious look at the new scheduling of Air Canada services. I raise this matter for the minister's consideration because it has created a certain amount of ill will and discontent in western Canada. Our business people in central and western Canada feel that they are being neglected or discriminated against in this regard.
I should like now to discuss, in concluding, the grade crossing fund which falls within the jurisdiction of the Department of Transport. There have been many, many instances in the last few years, and more particularly recently, of serious accidents that have taken place as a result of the lack of proper animated signals and safety devices at level or grade crossings. I think people are becoming more aware as
November 25, 1966

the days go by of the great loss of human resources through, for example, automobile accidents, particularly collisions with trains. The minister and his department should make more money available from the grade crossing fund for the provision of signals and all types of safety devices at our grade crossings. The process of treating applications should be speeded up so those areas that wish to avail themselves of these services and safety devices can obtain assistance as soon as possible.
We had the recent example of the serious accident which occurred at Port Hope. The minister announced to the house that he is looking into this tragedy. This is just one example. I believe this is an area where we have been a little lax. Therefore, I suggest to the minister that he and his officials clear up this area as quickly as possible.

Mr. Chairman, I am going to desert my usual cosmopolitan approach to life and be somewhat parochial for five minutes. First of all, I want to thank the minister for the courteous and complete way in which he has answered any queries I have brought to his direct attention. I appreciate the attention he has paid to my requests. In many instances, I have received not a brief letter but one of some length, which indicates that the minister has gone into the matter quite carefully.
I also wish to thank the deputy minister and staff of the department for their courteous attention to any matters I have brought to their notice. This applies also to the attention paid to matters raised by officials in British Columbia when there is occasionally a meeting in Vancouver, and when they are visiting my constituency.
First of all, Mr. Chairman, I should like to say that owing to the construction of the treaty projects on the Columbia river, many changes will be required in the aids to navigation on that river from the United States border to as far north as Revelstoke. This means that a good many of these aids will have to be relocated.
Traffic by water from the United States from as far south as Portland is increasing rapidly every year. Many of these boats go as far north as Revelstoke. Local traffic is increasing at an even greater rate owing to the growing ownership of pleasure craft and the increasing number of tugs employed in the forest and other industries.
I should like the minister to tell us who is responsible for the cost involved in the relocation of these aids to navigation on the river 23033-656
Supply-Transport
and lakes. Perhaps he will also tell us whether any surveys have been carried out with regard to the aids to navigation that will be required when the dams are completed, and what plans are being made for this relocation to take place so that there is no stoppage of navigation over any extended period of time. I should also like to bring to the minister's attention the fact that the relocation of aids to navigation will require the publication of new charts for the river in question.
I now wish to say a word or two about meteorological services. A number of persons in my constituency are weather observers; they make records and forward them to the appropriate department.
[DOT] (1:50 p.m.)
I would like to know how many were employed on this work in Kootenay West and at what annual cost. I might say that the completion of the treaty projects will no doubt cause a change in the climate, both as far as temperature is concerned and as far as rainfall and snowfall are concerned. I discussed this with competent persons who are very interested in the change in climate which occurs from these works of man, such as fiamg on rivers and lakes and things of that type. I do think that after the treaty projects are completed it will provide an opportunity for a competent person within the department to make a particular study of the effect on the climate of the works that have been completed in the area directly affected.
I would also suggest that there are a number of local community groups in the district which are interested in community television satellites. They have done excellent work in this field, and in some cases they have put quite a lot of money into these projects in an effort to bring C.B.C. programs to isolated communities. I do urge that these community groups, who are anxious to develop community satellite programs, receive every technical assistance possible from the minister's technical staff. They have received some in the past which they appreciate very much, and I trust they will receive every consideration in the future.
There is also an interesting development with respect to the improvement of the Nelson airfield in which I understand the city of Nelson, as well as other people in the surrounding areas, are very interested. I understand that the city made proposals some time ago for the transfer of certain land which was held in its name in connection with the Castlegar airfield in return for a grant from

November 25, 1966
Supply-Transport
the federal government for the development of the Nelson airport. I do not expect the minister will have time today to reply to these questions, but I would like to know what are the latest developments with respect to the application of the city for assistance in the development of their airport in return for the transfer of their rights in the Castlegar airfield. There are a few other smaller airports being supported as a result of local efforts, such as the ones at Nakusp and Kaslo, and there may be another one proposed. These airfields are developed strictly as the result of the efforts of the village or community concerned and I hope they will be able to receive all the technical assistance possible from the officials of the department.
I know that in a few cases preliminary surveys were made and estimates of costs have been given, as well as some ideas as to the suitability of the site and so on. I do urge that the same assistance be continued for these persons who are playing their part in the development of these smaller airports which are very necessary, particularly in a country such as ours.
Mr. Chairman, that is all I have to say at this time. I could go on at much greater length but I know there are a number of other hon. members who would like to say a few words before these estimates are passed.

Mr. Chairman, although I have discussed, on many occasions in the past, the matter which I want to submit to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill), I should like today to emphasize in particular, a crucial problem, facing not only the riding which I represent, but the whole city of Quebec, a problem which, since 1948, has beeen dealt with, on many occasions, by the municipal authorities as well as the hon. members representing this house, the Quebec East riding. Since 1948, I think that several representations have been made to the Board of Transport Commissioners and to the ministers of transport concerned, so that Quebec city could get rid of that chronic nuisance as we call the grade crossings.
Those who know Quebec city appreciate that all across the town and right in the center, there are eleven grade crossings which clearly paralyse the traffic between the north and the south of Quebec city, that is between the Limoilou and St. Roch districts.
On January 20, 1964, a first request was made to the Board of Transport Commissioners supported by rather good arguments,
[Mr. Herridge.l
asking for the removal of those grade crossings. On June 11, 1964, that same year, a second request was presented to the board and, following that request, arguments and replies provided by the Board of Transport Commissioners, on September 30, 1964, the Quebec municipal authorities asked to appear before the board. On November 16, replying to that request, Mr. Crump, refuted the arguments submitted in the previous request and denied politely the city of Quebec the right to appear before the board. According to the material which I have here with me, the request should not have been denied.
On October 21, 1965, a new request was presented and finally on November 7 last, a letter from Mr. G. P. Miller, which was published in the Quebec newspapers, said that the board could not consider the removal of the grade crossings in Quebec city, on the following grounds: the streets were too narrow and the motor car traffic over the grade crossings should first be controlled by the municipal authorities.
Mr. Chairman, I respectfully point out that this argument is not worth very much, if it is considered in its real context. Of course, Quebec city underwent a development similar to that of other cities and when the grade crossings were installed, obviously the traffic at that time was very light and the development to Quebec city from 1920 or 1925, if you wish had not been anticipated as in the case of all the other cities in Canada.
According to an investigation by the Quebec police department, from September 20, 1965 to October 1, and this is a good illustration of the traffic congestion at the grade crossings in Quebec city-I could for instance quote the following figures for September 20, the gates in operation on the eleven grade crossings concerned were raised 32 times for a total loss of time of 32 minutes to the car drivers who had to wait for the train to go by.
On Tuesday, September 21, 38 times, for a total of 52 minutes loss of time; 43 times for 65 minutes on September 22, and on September 23, 40 times for 61 minutes.
I do not wish to quote all these figures, Mr. Chairman, because I am aware of the fact that time for the debate is limited, and I would not like to deprive other members of the house who wish to discuss the subject of an opportunity to do so.
[DOT] (2:00 p.m.)
However, I cannot understand that, in 1966, the Board of Transport Commissioners does
November 25, 1966

not realize the necessity of solving the problem of grade crossings in the city of Quebec. The minister-and I thank him for this
appears to be much better disposed than the board itself since, on November 6 last, I was granted the honour of a special visit on his part in my riding of Quebec East. He wanted to see things for himself and have a look at all those grade crossings.
And I think the minister now understands the problem very well, because he stated that he was willing to co-operate with the city of Quebec authorities and do everything in his power to eliminate those crossings.
I thank the minister once again for being understanding and I feel the problem of grade crossings in Quebec city is crucial. We are no longer in 1920 or in 1940. Quebec city has developed, as well as the transportation services, and I believe it is time we realized that this problem deserves special attention.
It seems obvious that the party most concerned is the Canadian Pacific and that every time the municipal authorities of Quebec city made requests to that company, it always found good excuses in order to avoid solving that problem. I also understand that the city of Quebec has benefited by the advent of the railways and that, at that time, the citizens of Quebec city were no longer settlers and are even less so in 1966.
I believe also that the Canadian Pacific should understand that when its railway tracks were laid in Quebec city, the district of Limoilou did not exist north of those tracks and north of the St. Charles river. The Limoilou district now has some 75,000 inhabitants who ever day-and as indicated in the quotation which I have just given-some thirty times a day are deprived of lines of communication between the southern and northern parts of Quebec city on account of grade crossings and the passage of too many trains.
The most practical solution would be to move the line, the station in the first place, and then to remove the tracks to enable the trains to arrive in a new district of Quebec city, entirely in the western part of the city where fortunately, if this is done in the near future, there are still some available lots to build a fine station and practical access for railway tracks.
Limoilou and Saint-Roch are, of course, most directly involved. I am not now speaking strictly as the member for Quebec East. I would like my words to be considered as reflecting the opinion of the authorities of
23033-656J
Supply-Transport
Quebec city, and of all intermediary public bodies which joined the city in making representations in that sense many years ago.
I should like to emphasize, Mr. Chairman, that out of those 11 grade crossings, at least 6 are extremely important. Take the grade crossing on De la Couronne Street or on Dorchester Street, for instance, where 1400 vehicles per hour cross the tracks. Those interruptions cause a line-up of 70 vehicles each time, and that number even reaches 100 on occasion.
At the Dupont Street crossing, traffic is perhaps a little lighter, but it is nevertheless around 600 vehicles per hour. However, interruptions there are more frequent and last longer because marshalling operations are done in that area.
From 8 to 8.30 in the morning, there is an average of three interruptions lasting an average of four and a half minutes, during that single half hour.
Interruptions are more frequent and last longer at peak traffic hours. Saint-Roch in particular, is undergoing a complete change and major projects in what is called area No. 10 are now under way to renovate that district.
With the canalization of the St. Charles river-which has now been approved-it is obvious that those lines which run all along the St. Charles, on the south shore, will prevent the renovation of Saint-Roch unless they are removed.
The federal government is ready to spend over a million dollars for the construction of a dam. The federal and provincial governments, as well as the city of Quebec, are ready to spend huge amounts now and they have agreed to allocate $16 million to the canalization of the St. Charles river.
As members for Quebec and the vicinity, we all want to see that project become a reality and we want to co-operate with the municipal and provincial authorities so that the development of the St. Charles will be a success and the Saint-Roch district will become what we want it to be, a district where people will be proud to live, where apartment houses will be built and where the citizens of Quebec will be happy to go and live.
Those are not dreams, Mr. Chairman, they are projects which are becoming a reality and the C.P.R. tracks which run along the south shore of the river as well as the marshalling yards will just have to be moved from that district if the redevelopment of Saint-Roch;

November 25, 196$
Supply-Transport
and the city of Quebec in general is to be carried out.
Before ending my remarks, Mr. Chairman, I would like to point out the safety hazard which the level crossing at 22nd Street constitutes in my riding. On Sunday, November 6, the minister was able to see the safety hazard created by that crossing, in view of the fact that five schools and one church are located near it. I am sorry to inform the house that although we did not wish for that to happen and although we deeply regret it, last Wednesday night, a very serious accident occurred at that railway crossing when a young school-boy was struck by a train after school. Fortunately the child was not killed but it is easy to understand that things could have been different. That boy is now in hospital with a fractured leg and a spinal injury and it is not known yet what the results of that accident at the level crossing of 22nd Street will be.
Last Friday, I discussed with the mayor of Quebec city the immediate request which should be made to the Board of Transport Commissioners for the removal of that railway crossing. I trust that this question will be attended to immediately, so that an overhead crossing will be built and the danger which this 22nd Street crossing constitutes will be eliminated.
There had been no accidents so far; an accident occurred this week, and I hope such a tragedy will not be repeated; for that, immediate steps would have to be taken to improve the crossing by means of an overpass, and I trust that the Quebec municipal authorities will bring immediate attention to the request I have submitted to them.
In concluding my comments, I will add that I am pleased to have brought the railway crossing problem to the minister's attention. I think I will suggest to the authorities concerned, and to the public bodies of the city of Quebec, that they seek a new hearing with the Board of Transport Commissioners. I feel that with the necessary information, upon which I do not have time to elaborate today, we may be able to make them realize, once and for all, the necessity of eliminating all railway crossings in the city of Quebec and in Saint-Roch, because they are a crucial affliction and represent a public hazard not only for Quebec city residents but also for the numerous people who visit that picturesque city.

Mr. Chairman, I had a number of things I wanted to say, but I know the

minister is anxious to speak and I shall condense my remarks.
First of all, I wish to compliment the minister on his enunciation, earlier this fall, of the national air policy with its emphasis and recognition for the first time of the integral role that regional air carriers can and must play in the social and commercial development of a country as large and thinly populated as Canada. We, in Winnipeg south and southern Manitoba in general, welcome the minister's announcement with great enthusiasm. Regional carriers like TransAir are much encouraged by the minister's articulation of this new air policy. We will watch for further evidence of the government's good faith in this respect with great interest in the months immediately ahead.
The provision of incentives and encouragement to regional air carriers is long overdue. In the United States, some 10 of 12 regional air carriers now are operating in the black as a result of the climate of support for these carriers that has been created in that country.
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)
The only enlightened attitude possible in a country like the United States, and equally in a country like Canada, is an attitude of maximum possible support for the regional carrier. Having said that, I would now like to put a few questions on the record for the minister's consideration.
Merely because we are gratified in my constituency, Winnipeg South, and in my entire section of the country, at the government's new-found enlightenment on this subject of a national air policy and the importance of regional air carriers, the minister should not allow himself to lapse into an attitude of complacency. If he feels he now lives in a state of security as far as Winnipeg and the prairies are concerned, let me hasten to advise him that his impression is a false one.
1 said last February in this house that I felt Winnipeg was being at best ignored, at worst mistreated, in the transportation policies of the present administration, and I cannot see that in the intervening nine months the situation has improved very much. In fact, to some extent, it has deteriorated. Where, for example, are the long-promised escalators at the Winnipeg airport? Travellers at what surely is otherwise one of the finest airports on this continent, still must struggle with their hand baggage up and down long flights of stairs when going back and forth between the landing ramps and the respective waiting rooms at Winnipeg. These escalators, promised long
November 25, 1966

ago, and for which it is my impression financial provision was made long ago, still exist only in the realm of the imagination.
Perhaps the minister's flagging interest in this project could be revived somewhat if he would come out to Winnipeg by air and carry some of his baggage with him. Thousands of air travellers can assure him it is not good exercise; it is just plain inconvenient, and unnecessarily so.
What of the overseas rates by air to and from Winnipeg, a subject which I also discussed nine months ago? Manitoba air travellers are still the victims of what surely must be one of the most anachronistic and discriminatory policies in the whole field of transportation anywhere in the world.
As I pointed out then, a passenger flying from Winnipeg to London, England, via the direct Hudson Bay route, is charged a rate equivalent to that which he would pay were he to fly from Winnipeg to Montreal to London. This is a much higher rate, although the direct Hudson Bay route is hundreds of miles shorter than the Winnipeg-Montreal-London route.
This is what is known as the rule of normal ports of entry. In this case, under IATA regulations, Montreal is regarded as Canada's normal port of entry, and I ask this house what could be more anachronistic and unreasonable in this day of jet air travel.
All too often, in all too many situations, the geographic location of Winnipeg works against us-militates against our ambitions as a community. Why, then, when geography will work for us, as in this case, should we not be permitted to capitalize on our location and to reap such small advantage from it as may present itself. This government should be fighting for Winnipeg and the prairies in this regard, working to get the discriminatory regulations of IATA changed.
What of the need for research in the science of transportation and transportation policy? We were greatly heartened by a speech delivered, I believe, in Winnipeg earlier this fall on this very subject by the minister. This is another area in which western Canadians will be watching developments very closely.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that a school of transportation studies should be established, with the aid of the federal government, to serve this country's rapidly expanding need for experts and expertise in this vital field of activity.
Because of the background which Manitoba has in this field, because of its work over the
Supply-Transport
years on the freight rates issue and related question, because of its bank of statistical and empirical data, and because of its pool of expert transportation consultants already developed, I sumbit that the logical location for this proposed research centre and school is the province of Manitoba. There should, too, be a direct connection with the University of Manitoba.
The minister, as an old Manitoba University professor, hinted as much in his recent speech. He nods his approval almost imperceptibly now, which leads me to conclude that this project now has official ministerial sanction and will soon be a reality.
There is one other point I would mention, and it is one which, unlike the subject I have just mentioned, gives me no pleasure.
This is the question of national, transcontinental air service, into and out of Winnipeg, moving both east and west. In the first place, there is valid reason, sir, in my opinion, for examining now the possibility of permitting Canadian Pacific Airlines to expand its domestic service. Never has such a need been manifested more eloquently than during these past few days during the Air Canada strike, and during the last few days of August and the early part of September when the nation's railroads were strikebound.
Finally, there is the matter of equipment being used on east-west Air Canada flights on Air Canada's new winter schedule. This schedule which was already in effect before the current strike and presumably will be resumed when the strike is over.
A number of travellers have brought to my attention, and I must say I am inclined to agree with them, the fact that there has been a decline in the standard of equipment being used by Air Canada since November 1 on east-west domestic fi ghts.
In fact, one might ask the minister, in a paraphrase of a popular song of a few years ago: "Where have all the jet planes gone?" Could it be that they have gone south for the winter? Lately, the DC-8's and the DC-9's have been more and more scarce on Air Canada flights to and from western Canada, and the Viscounts and the Vanguards have been coming back into ever-increasing use. One cannot avoid the suspicion, Mr. Chairman, that this subtle shift in equipment is closely related to Air Canada's new landing rights in southern Florida and southern California, focal points of the winter tourist traffic. How can one escape the corollary

November 25, 196S
Supply-Transport
conclusion that this is another reflection of a long-standing attitude of cynicism on the part of Air Canada's president toward western Canada?

I would defer to the minister, but I am racing the clock so as to allow the Minister of Transport to speak. I am concluding my remarks at this point. The people of western Canada would, I am sure, appreciate it if the minister, a westerner by birth-
No.

-would look into this matter. If Mr. McGregor did not have the equipment to service southern California and southern Florida he should not have bid for the routes. As far as I can see, there is no reason on earth, or in the air, why the western Canadian traveller should be expected to bail Mr. McGregor out of his self-constructed predicament.

Mr. Chairman, I shall be brief, for I know that there are only 20 minutes left before the estimates of the Department of Transport are passed and I should like to draw the minister's attention to two very urgent cases in connection with the needs of my constituency.
First of all, I should like to discuss the Lachine canal. The Lachine canal has been a boon in past years but, in recent years, it has been a cause of trouble. I am told that in the last three years, about 100,000 tons of merchandise only were carried through the canal. I am also told that perhaps less than 50,000 tons will be carried throught it this year. The Lachine canal has reached the point where it must be closed and abandoned.
[DOT] (2:20 p.m.)
In the past, this canal has been a nightmare for people in the area including myself. Every year, one, two or three children drown in it. The wrong-doers who have something to hide use it as a cemetery, and therefore I renew my request to the minister that the Lachine canal be closed, once and for all, in view of the fact that it no longer serves the purposes for which it had been intended.
In the past, it has been a boon; I said so a moment ago-

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wonder would the hon. member permit me to interrupt him for a moment? It has been represented to me by a number of members on both sides of the chamber that they would like me to reply to a few of the points raised but my time expires, I am not too sorry to say, at 23 minutes to 3 o'clock, or so I am told.
I am in the hands of the committee. As Mackenzie King said to me many a time, no man was hung for something he did not say, so I will leave it to the committee to decide whether it wants to hear me.

Mr. Chairman, if the other hon. members agree to the minister's suggestion, I would ask the house to allow me two or three minutes, during which time I shall submit my requests to the minister, and then I shall resume my seat.
I shall not labour the point; however, at the present time, we are asking the closing of the Lachine canal, especially within the limits of the city of Montreal. Consultations are going on presently with the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority. I hope that these consultations, with the minister's support, will be brought to a successful conclusion and that the city of Montreal will be able to buy this famed canal for the price of $1, without too many strings attached, to use it for purposes such as subway, water and sewer systems, express-way.
Now, Mr. Chairman, without further ado I come to my second request. It has to do with the removal of the Canadian National Railways tracks, which run through part of my constituency, and I believe it is proper to ask that they be removed, since, actually, they do not go beyond Windsor Street.
That 243-acre area is being renovated and it would be advisable-it is even essential, and I trust that the minister will use his authority and make the recommendation-that the C.N.R. tracks which presently end at Windsor Street, stop more to the west, that is at Saint-Remi Street, from where the freight could be carried by truck.
I would like to speak further, Mr. Chairman, but I cannot in view of the limited time at our disposal. However, I would appreciate it if the minister took my two requests into serious consideration: the closing of Lachine canal within the limits of the city of Montreal and its sale to the city of Montreal for the sum of $1; the removal of C.N.R. tracks between St. James and Notre Dame Streets, from Saint-Remi to Windsor Streets.
November 25, 1966

I also wish to warn the minister that I have been told of a Canadian Pacific Railways application for the construction of railway lines on the Lachine canal. I understand that the Board of Transport Commissioners is presently considering the application; I trust the minister will look into the matter and make sure that the C.P.R.'s request is denied.
Mr. Chairman, this is all for the time being. I would have liked to elaborate further, but nevertheless I hope the minister will give us encouraging replies with respect to those two requests that I am making on behalf of the city of Montreal.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am not going to make any original observations of any kind. I am only going to try to deal with as many of the points raised by members of the committee as I can in the time available. I may say that I feel, if not complacent, rather encouraged-I say this in particular to the hon. member for Winnipeg South-by what on the whole has been the rather friendly attitude during discussion of my estimates. I hope that attitude may persist even after I have spoken
The hon. member for Kindersley made one or two very interesting points. I think he was right in saying that I became almost more
Supply-Transport
impatient than he did about the delays with respect to local airports. One of the difficulties we do have in this matter is that, unfortunately, there are more things to do in this country than there are resources with which to do them.
With reference to Bay d'Espoir which, although it is pronounced despair does not mean despair but actually means hope, I would point out that there is a huge power development going on there. There was no road leading to it and the airport was absolutely essential to carry in materials. In any event, this work was done before the policy came into operation this year. In this connection, I think Saskatchewan is not doing at all badly if one looks at all figures, but unfortunately I cannot take the time now to put them on record.
With reference to railway grade crossings, I may say that the organization of mayors and municipalities at its meeting with the cabinet yesterday made certain representations about railway crossings. I assured them that as soon as the new transport commission was established I would ask it, or if it took too long to establish, I would ask the Board of Transport Commissioners, to make a study of alternative approaches to this problem.
The hon. member for Quebec East also spoke about this problem. I may tell the committee I went to Quebec city with him and we saw every crossing, except one or two, in the whole city one Sunday morning. I hope it was a pious thing to do, because it was in an effort to try to keep people alive. The situation in Quebec city is quite incredible. You have to see it, but even then you can hardly believe it. I think the hon. member has the right idea when he suggests taking the railway lines out of the city and putting the station in another place. It might be a great deal cheaper than dealing with all those crossings, and this approach might be applicable to Sault Ste. Marie as well as a lot of other places.
I would like to make a long speech about seaway tolls but if I did I would not have time to say anything about anything else. I just want to make two points. The first is that the seaway is just about up to capacity now, and if we are going to carry large, additional quantities of grain and other bulk commodities through it, we will have to expand the seaway.
I doubt if we are going to get this parliament to agree to expanding the seaway to the degree it should be expanded unless there are reasonable tolls charged. I do not think it is fair to ask the voters and taxpayers of Halifax and Prince Rupert to pay for something which can be of no real benefit to them. Adequate

November 25, 1966
Supply-Transport
tolls on the seaway will enable us to expand the Welland canal and the seaway so that bigger vessels can be used to carry grain, which would be an advantage to the constituents of the hon. member for Kindersley. They have broad horizons out there. I hope they will take a broad and long view of this and, if they do, I am sure they will agree with me.
The hon. member for Skeena referred to two subjects, one of which I am going to leave to my honourable and learned friend, the Minister without Portfolio, who has been making a special study of it, to deal with. I have a report, which I am going to send the hon. gentleman, on the delays that have been occasioned by the recent troubles with the longshoremen in Vancouver harbour. Up to now, they do not seem to have been serious enough to cause hardship but only to cause annoyance.
One of the difficulties is that when one ship got to Prince Rupert the longshoremen there were unwilling to unload it. I trust the hon. gentleman will use his influence, which I am sure is very great with them, to see that they unload it.
I will trade my influence in that regard for the minister's influence to get a new grain elevator built in Prince Rupert.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport

The hon. member for Medicine Hat said, notwithstanding the good job which has been done by the railways and others in respect of the movement of grain, he was not altogether happy about the distribution of the movements. I am not altogether happy either, and I know the Minister of Finance is of the same opinion. We need more facilities for the movement of grain. These can be provided only at a certain pace. We are trying to step up the pace in every way we can. I am glad that the hon. gentleman did not suggest that we have a controller. I do not think that would work. I believe that in the last two years the co-ordination has been pretty good. The difficulty is that the people who are good at co-ordinating these things are the same people who are doing the operation and if they are attending too many meetings they do not have the time to get on with the job of moving the grain. The matter will never be solved of course until we have better facilities for doing so.
In connection with the air service at Medicine Hat, I think and I hope this will be one of the places which will get better service as a result of the announcement recently made concerning the regional air policy.
I cannot say how much I sympathize with the hon. member for Cochrane, who is one of my dearest friends. I know that there is no other member in this house who serves his constituents more faithfully than he.
How does a person get praise like that?

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, with the indulgence of the committee, one cannot really embrace this important subject in one minute. In reply to the hon. member for Skeena, I can say this government believes that life is more important than property on the rivers and lakes. We have had a series of meetings and the departmental officials have been extremely busy improving the safety features and traffic control system on the St. Lawrence river channel.
With regard to the question raised concerning the Manseau 101 barge case, I might say that the provincial inquiry now is under way. So far as I know it has not yet been completed. The formal inquiry before Mr. Justice Noel which has been set up by the Department of Transport is not a limited inquiry. Its terms of reference are sufficiently large to relate to marine safety. I know the issue my hon. friend had in mind. If the seamen, through the Seafarers' International Union, wish to bring their case before the commissioner they must make application in the usual way, because he is in charge of the inquiry. At the last meeting on marine safety we studied the problem of manning ships. The developments are reaching a stage when the department may have to consider publishing regulations affecting safety. This derives from technological change when crews might be cut to a point when safety would be endangered. It is not so much the size of the crew but rather the number of men on watch or alert at any one time or the factor of fatigue. Other matters are properly for collective bargaining. On another occasion I hope to have an opportunity to expand further on this particular subject.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, because I do not wish to deny other members the opportunity of making their own remarks concerning the Department of Agriculture, I shall be as brief as possible.
However, I wish to take this opportunity to draw to the minister's attention a matter of great importance. Last week I met a business man interested in the vegetable canning industry. He was telling me that a large quantity of canned tomatoes is coming in from Italy. The results of such large-scale imports are that no buyers were interested in our 1966 production which is still in storage. As a result all the farmers in my riding interested in growing tomatoes for canning purposes are much concerned and look forward to next year's crop with much apprehension.
I wish to draw the attention of the minister to that fact, for, in my riding, many farmers derive their income from tomato growing, and should foreign competition prevent the sale of our own products it would be detrimental, first, to the 40 or 50 employees of that particular cannery and, second, to employees working in other canneries who would also be deprived of gainful employment.
I would also like to talk briefly about the dairy industry. The minister knows quite well that the dairy industry for eastern farmers and, possibly, for Quebec farmers particularly, is a very important one. Our farmers derive about 40 per cent of their revenues from

the dairy industry and, because of the reluctance on the part of the minister to announce his dairy policy in the last two years, a feeling of uncertainty has developed in the minds of our farmers, to such an extent that in many cases herds have been reduced. Farmers have been forced to take such a decision, because they could not depend on adequate revenues.
For example, a comparison between 1957 and 1966 shows that in 1957 herds numbered
3.098.000	head, compared with 2,799,000 only in 1966. It is true that production methods have improved greatly and, consequently, that milk production may not be comparable, nowadays, we can produce as much milk with fewer cows than in the past.
This reduction in the number of cattle is an undeniable indication of concern among farmers, resulting in a switch from dairy production to other farming activities.
For instance, butter production, which reached 139,330,000 pounds, dropped to 131,-
611,000	pounds in 1965. These figures appear in a published booklet entitled "Dairy Farmers of Canada"-1966 edition.
Mr. Chairman, it is to be expected that if the milk production and the number of milch cows keep going down year after year, butter may eventually become scarce in Canada. We shall then probably have to supply ourselves elsewhere, whereas it seems natural that a country as rich as Canada should be able to produce the butter it needs.
In order to show that imports keep increasing, allow me to point out, Mr. Chairman, that in 1956, Canada imported 8,885,000 pounds of cheese, while in 1965, the figure reached
17.794.000	pounds.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the hon. member how many pounds of butter were in storage in 1956?

In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I would like to call the attention of the minister to the fact that in order to have a sound product, it is essential for farmers to have healthy cattle. I see in the monthly letter of the Department of Agriculture that brucellosis is finally under control. This is good news for farmers, because this contagious disease has made them lose thousands of dollars. The price of purebred cattle is constantly increasing and this is the reason why I would ask the minister to amend the legislation on epizootic diseases, in order that farmers may be better paid when they are unfortunate enough to have a diseased herd.
When we were in power, we had raised considerably the allowance for lost animals, and I think the minister could help the people by doing the same thing, that is, by raising the allowance paid for slaughtered animals under the Animal Contagious Diseases Act, because the farmers must oay much more for them.
Supply-Agriculture
I do not need to remind the minister also that he has a lot to do if he wants to help the farmers. For example, he could see to it that the prices of farm machinery are more proportionate to the revenue from the sale of products. The prices of farm machinery are always increasing and one of the reasons for this is probably the 11 per cent tax imposed upon building materials.
Therefore, I should like in conclusion to ask the minister to put pressure upon his colleague the Minister of Finance and Receiver General (Mr. Sharp), so that this 11 per cent tax may be abolished as soon as possible.

Mr. Chairman, under the system that we have now I am not going to be too long-winded in dealing with this problem. It is not that the situation in agriculture is any better now than it has been, but my remarks shall be brief because of the time factor involved. I should like to mention several things that I think are plaguing the farmers today. I have been informed that the Ontario Farmers Union have passed a major piece of legislation in their own councils whereby farmer groups will have the right to call strikes, not on an over-all basis but in relation to a particular product that may be experiencing severe difficulty. Therefore, the minister will have to face these problems as they arise.
The dairy industry has been mentioned. I do not want to pursue that matter at this time. However, I believe the problems of the dairy industry are not solved. I should like to congratulate the minister and his officials on the change that has been made in paying the cream subsidy on a monthly basis. A member of parliament who has cream producers in his area knows that the old system of payment caused more consternation and division among farmers than anything else.
In the last election campaign the Liberal party stated that they intended to dispose of the small farmer and could do this through the market place. To some extent this policy has been carried out as far as cream producers are concerned. Certainly the policy which provided a three-month waiting period for a subsidy cheque, rather than receiving it monthly, assisted the transfer-and perhaps this in some measure was justified-of a large number of cream producers to secondary milk marketing. Rather than separating the milk on the farm, these producers were persuaded as a result of this policy to get into the secondary milk field. In my area this policy has

November 25, 1966
Supp ly-Agriculture
resulted in the establishment of a new cheese factory, which will double the cheese production in Timiskaming. I believe this is largely related to the policy of the government with respect to farm-separated cream, which policy has been maintained for a number of years.
There are other major problems facing agriculture. We are facing the problem that was mentioned briefly a few moments ago, namely, the shortage of butter. In my opinion, Canada has now changed from a country plagued with agricultural surpluses to one that may have to give much greater consideration to how we can produce enough of any given commodity, on a stable basis, to meet our commitments in the export markets we have built up and the domestic demands.
When we look back over the last 10 years of the operation of the stabilization board in regard to butter, we see that the situation has been a strange one. We remember the scandals that took place in British Columbia in this field, and the plant that burned down in the province of Quebec a few years ago. What occurred in this connection was rather covered up. It is strange when we recall that we have been selling butter oil, rendered butter, at a price that obviously did not cover the cost of production let alone the money which the federal government put into this commodity. After many years of storing this commodity we had to liquidate it in a market in which there was really no demand. I am sure we will be reminded of this by the people of Canada who had to pay for this costly program, when we are now faced with the possibility of importing butter this year to meet our domestic requirements. The short range aspect of our policy is certainly indicated in this example.
The fact that we may have to import large quantities of tobacco indicates that our problems in this field have not been solved. In order to maintain a reasonable price, producers of this commodity had to cut down their acreages. They had to do this in a very strict and dictatorial manner which caused a great deal of commotion in the tobacco producing areas, particularly in respect of those who were on the outside rather than the inside.
There is something the government will have to think about, particularly the Minister of Agriculture, as indicated by the following passage in one of the publications of the department, namely, "News From The Canada Department of Agriculture." This publication is for the week ending November 25, and over the minister's signature, in the last section,

under the heading "Marketing Boards" it reads:
Ottawa, November 25,	1966-There were 88
marketing boards for farm products registered in nine provinces in 1964. according to a report issued by CDA's economics branch. Number of members, at 211,000 was unchanged from the previous year.
The value of products under the jurisdiction of the 73 boards which reported their activities for that year to the branch amounted to $488 million- about 14 per cent of farm cash income for the whole country.
I have for a long time been advocating the establishment, under the federal Department of Agriculture, of federal marketing boards. I am well aware of provincial autonomy in this respect and the constitutional limitations on marketing legislation. But I think it is time the Department of Agriculture in Ottawa called a conference with the provincial ministers of agriculture and decided under what form of marketing legislation we could introduce national marketing boards.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)
It seems to me that the fight a few months ago between the provincial ministers of agriculture in Quebec and Ontario and the federal Minister of Agriculture highlighted the fact that if the provincial agricultural ministers are going to take steps to correct a situation in their provinces they are likely to hurt farmers in another area and make the position of the federal government untenable. We will have to operate as "big brother" to the provinces which are faced with the same problem but deal with it in a different manner. I believe that if agriculture is to be a vibrant industry in Canada, as I am sure everyone wishes it to be, market legislation will have to play an increasing role. It has always struck me as being odd to find the province of Ontario operating in Europe through the cheese marketing board. It did an excellent job over the years, but it has always seemed to me that this was the responsibility of a national board because when we sell Ontario cheese in England it might deprive the cheese producers in the province of Quebec of the opportunity of selling their cheese in that market. As soon as they found themselves with a surplus, the price dropped. The market in Ontario was undercut and the gains which they made were really taken away from them, so they had to compensate themselves for the sales they were making.
In my opinion this is true of most farm marketing legislation where export commodities are involved. The advantages of marketing legislation on a federal basis can best be
November 25, 1966

exemplified by the wheat board and the excellent job which they have been able to do, not only for the provinces of Saskatchewan and Manitoba but for all the prairie provinces. These advantages have now been extended beyond those provinces.
I do not know whether any changes in marketing legislation will take place, but I think the Canadian public are very interested in the whole problem. The price of wheat in western Canada, which is tied to international agreements, is exceptionally low in terms of the cost of production to the farmers. This cost of production is rising without compensation being made to the farmers in terms of sales. Over the years there has been much discussion regarding the matter of a two-price system for wheat, but recently the government has studiously steered away from that course.
They promised it in 1963.

Yes, they did, but as you know there are cabinet ministers in the government who say that promises made during election campaigns are not promises at all; they are election bait and after the election the best thing to do is to forget about them as soon as possible. I think the minister would be well advised to reconsider the two-price system in relation to the export position of Canada. Otherwise, one of these days we will find that the United States will dispose of the restriction under their law whereby there is no minimum price on wheat no matter where the sales are made. This will increase the price putting the United States in a non-competitive position in many of the markets. One of these days this law might be changed, and then Canada will have to fight for its life in the international field. I think we should be prepared to consider our export market in relation to the domestic market, which would result in a better deal for the western farmers and would ensure our competitive position. I suggest that this should be done in many fields, and if we are to be the breadbasket of the world, as we all think we should and we can, then we will have to consider the export of our agricultural commodities on a national basis. This can only be done under national marketing legislation. If changes are to be made in our constitution, then let us start by making overtures to the provinces to extend our legislation in this field.
One of the major problems affecting the agricultural producers in the whole of our country is the pricing of farm machinery. I was pleased to note that on May 27, 1966 the
Supply-Agriculture
minister appointed a farm machinery inquiry under the leadership of Clarence L. Barber, head of the economic division of the University of Manitoba. In my opinion this man is highly qualified to conduct such an inquiry. Such an inquiry is more properly conducted by a royal commission rather than a committee of the House of Commons which has already instituted such an inquiry on two occasions without conclusions having been reached in either case. The factors which are to be studied include the impact of financing, distribution and servicing costs of farm machinery. The commission was also asked to look into the agricultural machinery industry in Canada, and in the export markets, as compared to the agricultural machinery industries in other countries. It is interesting to note that the government has never really looked at this aspect of the farm machinery industry because if they had they would not have been so surprised at the fact that the automobile pact which was recently negotiated has not served the interests of Canada.
A similar pact was concluded on an international basis many years before whereby duty on farm machinery was removed regardless of where it was produced or sold. I am told that it is possible to buy a tractor in India and have it delivered in Canada duty-free. All you have to pay is the cost of transportation. It is interesting to note in this field that the largest agricultural implement industry is Canadian. The other day one of my colleagues, in speaking about other Canadian companies including the Trans-Canada Pipe Lines, said that just because it was a Canadian company that did not make it good. There are just as many Canadian companies that are corporately bad as there are foreign companies. The same is true of the Massey-Harris Company, the largest agricultural implement producer. As was indicated in the last study, this company was only producing two farm implements in Canada, and all the rest were produced somewhere else.
The 1966 inquiry will also look into measures which will contribute to the expansion of an efficient production of agricultural machinery, the attainment of technological advances, the improvement of distribution, study, this company was only producing two financing and servicing facilities, and the enhancement of the industry's competitive position so that Canadian farmers would be ensured most favourable prices for, and availability of, machinery parts.

November 25, 1966
Supply-Agriculture
I had the doubtful honour of having been a member of the committees on agriculture and colonization in the years 1960 and 1961. It is interesting to note that there was no particular difference between their terms of reference. Their terms of reference read as follows:
Tuesday, March 14, 1961
Resolved,-That the standing committee on agriculture and colonization be empowered to continue its inquiry into the question of prices of farm machinery as recommended by the said committee in its fourth report presented to the house July 28, 1960, and that the committee's minutes of proceedings and evidence with regard to this inquiry at the last session be referred to the said committee.
In other words, the committee asked that it be reconstituted and that the business of the committee be continued. The following problems were investigated by the committee, as reported in the minutes of the committee on page 1479 of the committee report of September 26, 1961:
Your committee has investigated the following aspects of farm machinery prices:
1.	Costs of manufacturing farm machinery, including labour (wages and salaries), materials, overhead and profits;
2.	Costs of distributing farm machinery, including the margins earned by dealers and transportation costs;
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
3.	Other costs of ownership of farm machinery, such as charges for credit;
4.	The organization of the farm machinery industry and market in North America.
It goes on:
Your Committee reports that it has met 32 times and feels, due to the wide scope of the questions considered, further study is necessary to determine the effect on the prices of farm machinery and repairs of the following:
(a)	If farmers are receiving the full advantage of a free trade market in farm machinery
(b)	Cost of distribution of farm machinery
(c)	Cost and standardization of parts
(d)	Standardization of farm machinery
(e)	Credit arrangements
(f)	The reluctance of machine manufacturers to provide details of their costs, which are regarded as being of a competitive nature
(g)	Different opinions of the witnesses as to the productivity of labour as compared to increase in wages.
Further study is also required because of the following:
(a)	The necessity of recalling some witnesses
(b)	Other witnesses yet to be heard.
The committee agreed and the house agreed that the committee should continue in session in 1962, until it was able to make recommendations. What was recommended did not take

place. The minister has written letters to the farm implement industry indicating that he wanted to do something about the promise he made to the farmers, when he made his trip to western Canada last year. He said he would do something about the prices farmers had to pay for things, because farmers were caught in the cost-price squeeze and high farm machinery costs.
There is an order of the house for the tabling of documents and letters received from the farm implement companies. That order was made after the companies increased their machinery prices. I want to know if the minister intends to table those letters.
The minister, as the committee found, knows that we cannot make any decision about solving the difficulties if we do not have available the information on which the government ought to base its decision. Outside influences, it is true, affect farm machinery costs. The government of Saskatchewan has done much research into new implements. Before certain implements are licensed for sale in Saskatchewan they have to meet certain tests. This government very magnanimously applauded the decision of the premier of Saskatchewan to turn this kind of service over-and this is the only service like this in Canada, and certainly, it is the only one I am aware of operating to the extent of the Saskatchewan service-to the University of Saskatchewan without providing facilities to carry out the required research, or the power to licence or reject any particular implement.
It is true that in the province of Quebec the Co-op Federee has been able to buy in bulk a number of commodities, as has the C.C.I.L. in western Canada. These organizations were able to buy on a co-operative basis and sell to their members at lower commodity prices.
In any case, are organizations such as these making an impact on farm machinery costs in the initial stage? What they do has no effect on the farm machinery companies. This matter is critical, because in my area most farmers cannot buy a $12,000 combine, nor a $6,000 or $7,000 tractor. They cannot pay cash for these things, and they have to buy them on the instalment plan over a long period. The 25 per cent increase which is taking place because of government legislation on the order paper relating to bank loans hits these farmers hard.
This government has not helped the situation, but seems to have gone out of its way to help raise the cost of farm machinery. It has shown an inability to maintain that pressure that the former government maintained-and
November 25, 1966



I will give them credit for that-on the farm machinery companies forcing them to keep their prices down. That pressure was maintained through the agriculture and colonization committee.
The committee may not have done anything but it did keep down the prices of farm machinery for at least two or three years. In my opinion, it kept them down for five years. The farm machinery companies nibbled away at increases during the time, but now they have stopped nibbling. They have become bold and they say, "We will raise our prices and the government be damned." The inquiry presently being conducted will have no more success than previous inquiries. For instance, we find that Massey-Ferguson has implement parts manufactured all over the world, in France, South America, India, China, and it is exporting these commodities to Canada.
Our farmers who are plagued with transportation costs which increase the prices of their produce in the market, have to buy imported machinery, on which transportation costs have to be paid. They are caught in a squeeze, and are without any protection.
If the Minister of Agriculture goes home to Renfrew-he has had to return home, and I was more fortunate than he was in that regard-he will find many farmers who try to live on $2,000 or $3,000 a year are having a difficult time. It is no problem for the Minister of Agriculture to find that the farms of western Canada are conducted more as businesses than as family farms. For instance, they have accountants, because a quarter of a cent, when multiplied a thousandfold, makes a great difference. Many of the farms in western Canada are different from those in the area of Renfrew.
The little farmer, caught in the cost price squeeze, is blamed by consumers across the country for the rising cost of living. The farmer cannot do anything. In fact, he gets less now for his produce and he has to pay more for his machinery, but the public blames him for increased commodity prices in the market.
Labour, it is interesting to note, has been interested in this problem. Labour was interested at the time of the previous hearings and for a very selfish reason, in my opinion. You may remember the story of Walter Reuther attending at the Ford automobile factory in Detroit. The head of the company took him round the floor and showed him one of the automated machines they used to make cars. He said, "How will you collect dues from this
Supply-Agriculture
machine? It will be difficult to collect dues, will it not?"
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
Mr. Reuther said: That is true. It will be a real problem. But how are you going to sell automobiles to these machines?
We can see this situation developing today. Many more people would like to buy these machines but are unable to so because present prices, the product of the profit motive, are prohibitive. No matter how small the operation, many farmers would like to mechanize their farms. In my area it is hard to find a farmer today who owns a team of horses and a wagon. He hauls his products in a truck. If his time is worth anything, he cannot afford to spend it on the road with a team of horses. So, it is necessary to merchandise even small farms.
I believe the minister will need to consider this question in a more positive way than by writing letters to farm machinery companies and receiving replies which obviously call for further inquiry on his part. The income received from the sale of agricultural commodities has risen very little in recent years, while farm costs have been increasing sharply as can be ascertained by noting the income which is left in the farmer's hands.
I have been going back over some of the literature presented to the farm inquiry. Figures published by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics relative to the operating and other expenses of farmers in Canada show that in 1947 the cash income of the average farm amounted to $2,226 out of which $966 or 43 per cent had to be spent in operating costs, leaving a net income of $1,260. Take the figures for what was probably the best year, 1949. Cash income was $2,500, operating expenses were $1,100 or 46 per cent of cash income and net income amounted to $1,400. By 1951, net income amounted to $2,154 and 50 per cent of the cash income was taken up by operating expenses.
In 1959, the last year for which figures are recorded here, cash income amounted to $2,808, and operating expenses $1,890 or 67.3 per cent, leaving a net income of $918. In other words, the farmer was paying $1,800 to operate his farm in 1959 whereas in 1947 it cost him less than $1,000. Nevertheless his income in 1959 was $100 less than it had been in 1947. Net income had decreased by $100, though the cost of operation had more than doubled in a 12-year period.
If these figures were projected into later years I expect we would find that the same

trend had continued. In agriculture, we have become victims of the market place and of the farm machinery industry. Now, the situation has been made worse by the imposition of higher interest rates on money which farmers need to borrow for operating expenses or farm improvements. This government has really lifted the ceiling from interest rates, whether on short term loans or on loans for long term capital expenditure. The results will probably become evident to all farmers by next spring.
I do not want to say that I am in favour of strikes in the farm industry. But I am pleased that the farmers of Ontario have decided to do something about their problems. If the only thing they accomplish is to tell the people of Ontario and the people of Canada that they have a grievance, and outline some of the solutions which they feel would be to their advantage, then I believe they will have accomplished a great deal. And if the farmers go so far as to organize pressure groups and strikes, I believe the minister will be unable to ignore those developments, and something good may come of them.
